quick: Category C; use if benefit justifies risk
Excreted in milk; use with caution
Reduce dose / extend interval; monitor levels
Limit; added hepatic and neuropathy risk
summary: Ethambutol is a first-line bacteriostatic anti-tuberculosis drug always used in combination, never alone. Initial treatment is 15 mg/kg once daily (25 mg/kg in retreatment). The hallmark toxicity is dose- and duration-related optic neuritis with decreased visual acuity and red-green color blindness, requiring vision monitoring.
indications: Treatment of pulmonary tuberculosis, in combination with at least one other antitubercular drug
Treatment of other mycobacterial infections (e.g., Mycobacterium avium complex) as part of combination therapy

dosage.n: Always with at least one other anti-TB drug

dosage.d: 25 mg/kg once daily for 60 days, then reduce to 15 mg/kg once daily
dosage.n: With other anti-TB drugs; monitor eyes monthly at 25 mg/kg

dosage.d: Not recommended (safe use not established) per US label
dosage.n: WHO uses ~20 mg/kg in children where required

admin: Never use ethambutol alone; always combine with at least one other anti-TB drug
Administer once every 24 hours; absorption not significantly affected by food
Continue until bacteriologic conversion is permanent and maximal clinical improvement occurs
Perform baseline and periodic visual acuity and color discrimination testing
Reduce dose and lengthen interval in renal impairment
moa: Inhibits arabinosyl transferases (encoded by the embAB genes) involved in synthesis of arabinogalactan, an essential component of the mycobacterial cell wall. Disruption of cell-wall biosynthesis is bacteriostatic against actively dividing Mycobacterium tuberculosis and other mycobacteria.

absolute: Optic neuritis (unless clinical judgment determines it may be used)
Patients unable to report visual symptoms (young children, unconscious)

preg: Pregnancy Category C. Adequate well-controlled studies are lacking; ophthalmic abnormalities reported in some infants of women on anti-TB therapy including ethambutol. Use only if the potential benefit justifies the potential risk; generally considered acceptable in TB treatment during pregnancy.
lact: Ethambutol is excreted in breast milk in concentrations similar to maternal plasma. Use with caution; generally considered compatible during TB treatment.
renal: Excreted largely unchanged by the kidneys; reduce dose or extend the dosing interval in renal impairment and monitor serum levels and visual function closely.
hepatic: Hepatotoxicity including fatalities has been reported. Perform baseline and periodic assessment of hepatic function, especially in combination regimens with other hepatotoxic anti-TB drugs.

moderate: Aluminum hydroxide antacids - may delay and reduce absorption
Concomitant hepatotoxic anti-TB drugs (isoniazid, rifampin, pyrazinamide) - additive hepatotoxicity
minor: Neurotoxic drugs - possible additive peripheral neuropathy
interactions.food: Absorption is not significantly altered by food.
interactions.alcohol: Limit; increases hepatotoxicity and neuropathy risk within TB regimens.
interactions.diagnostics: May increase serum uric acid; can elevate liver enzymes.

common: Elevated serum uric acid (may precipitate gout)
emergency: Irreversible blindness from untreated optic neuritis

monitoring: Baseline and periodic visual acuity and red-green color discrimination (monthly at high dose/long therapy)
Serum uric acid in patients with gout risk
counsel: Report any change in vision, blurring or difficulty seeing red/green immediately
Take once daily; complete the full TB course with companion drugs
Report joint pain (gout) or signs of liver trouble (yellow skin, dark urine)
pk: Store at controlled room temperature; protect from moisture
pearls: Optic neuritis is dose- and duration-related; usually reversible if caught early - monitor vision and counsel patients.
Always used in combination, never as monotherapy.
Not recommended in children <13 years (US label) as they cannot reliably report visual changes.
Reduce dose in renal impairment - largely renally cleared.
missed: Take the missed dose when remembered on the same day; if it is nearly time for the next dose, skip it and resume the once-daily schedule. Do not double up. Adherence to the full TB regimen is essential.
overdose: Limited data; overdose may worsen optic and gastrointestinal toxicity. Treat supportively with gastric decontamination if early, and monitor visual and renal function. No specific antidote; hemodialysis can remove ethambutol.
